feedback: If a selection is vague or off-topic, ask: 'Does that pattern actually answer the question?' and let the learner reselect.
When the on-point data points are selected, lock in the claim with those numbers attached so the learner sees the completed claim–evidence link.
If the learner picks only one number, ask whether a single value or the pattern across the set is the stronger evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific answer is a claim built from and backed by the right specific evidence, not a general impression or prior belief; supplying the actual numbers makes the difference between 'because I think so' and 'because the data shows 9 versus 2' concrete.
learnerActions: Read a posed question such as 'Does light help plants grow?' alongside the class results shown as a results table and bar chart.

Examine the table and bar chart to find the pattern first, then state your answer as a claim and select the exact data points or bars that show it (e.g. the light-grown and dark-grown bars), connecting them to your claim.

Attach the specific numbers from your class results to your claim. For example, if the results showed 9 cm in light versus 2 cm in the dark, it would read 'Light helps plants grow because the data shows 9 cm in light versus 2 cm in the dark.' In real trials, seedlings grown in the dark can be taller than those in light but pale and spindly, so make your claim from the results and measures you actually have.
When a vague or irrelevant selection is made, respond to the prompt 'Does that pattern actually answer the question?' and choose again.
Try a second dataset where the pattern needs looking for (several values, not one obvious pair) so you must genuinely interpret rather than read a label.
activities.title: Build your claim from the data (data-explorer)

feedback: If the learner lists numbers without interpreting, prompt: 'Which places have the most? The fewest? What do the busy places have in common?'
If the learner answers from prior belief (e.g. 'minibeasts like flowers'), point back to the specific counts as the evidence that must support the answer.
If the learner uses only one number (just 'path 1' or just 'logs 12'), ask them to use the spread of values across all the places to establish the pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: A strong evidence-based answer identifies the overall trend (far more minibeasts found in the sheltered spots — logs 12, leaves 10, long grass 8 — than on the open path, 1), quotes those specific numbers, and ties the pattern back to the question rather than relying on prior belief or a single cherry-picked figure. The counts fit the idea that minibeasts prefer damp, sheltered places, but only if those spots really were damper and every place was searched in the same way, because the chart itself records counts, not dampness.
learnerActions: Study a chart of minibeasts found in different places: under logs 12, in long grass 8, on the open path 1, under leaves 10.
Answer the question 'Do minibeasts prefer damp, sheltered places?' by stating the pattern you see.
Point to the specific counts you would use as evidence and explain why those numbers do the work.
Explain how the pattern helps answer the question, not just read the numbers aloud.
Consider a what-if: 'If the open path had 15 minibeasts, would that change your answer? Which numbers are doing the work?'
activities.title: Spot the pattern and point to your numbers (open probe)

feedback: For a mismatched claim and data point, ask the learner to check whether that pattern actually relates to the question asked.
When a statement is miscategorised, prompt: 'Is this the raw data we collected, or what we think it means?'
activities.intendedInsight: Distinguishing an observation from its meaning, and knowing which specific data supports which claim, reinforces the claim–evidence link and plants the observation-versus-interpretation distinction.
learnerActions: Answer 'Which data best answers this question?' by selecting the data point that supports a given claim.
Match several claims to the specific data points that support each one.
Sort statements into two piles: 'claim' (what we conclude) versus 'evidence' (the raw data/observation that supports it).
activities.title: Claim or evidence? Matching and sorting

feedback: If the learner gives a vague justification, the persona asks again for the specific numbers or observations behind the claim.
Affirm when the learner names a specific data point and ties it to the question.
activities.intendedInsight: An answer must be backed by specific evidence the learner can name; being asked 'what's your evidence?' builds the habit of citing data rather than asserting a belief.
learnerActions: Share a tentative answer to a scientific question posed by a curious-scientist persona.
Respond to repeated prompts: 'How do you know? What's your evidence? What in the results makes you say that?'
Revise your answer so it names specific data points rather than 'because I could tell' or 'it just did'.
activities.title: How do you know? (evidence-probing dialogue)
